'''Violet Bushwick Haas''' (November 23, 1926 – January 21, 1986) was an American applied mathematician specializing in [[control theory]] and [[optimal estimation]] who became a professor of electrical engineering at [[Purdue University College of Engineering]].

== Early life and education ==
Haas was born November 23, 1926, in [[Brooklyn]].{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1986|p=12}} She completed a A.B. in mathematics{{sfn|''The Indianapolis Star''|1986|p=55}} at [[Brooklyn College]] in 1947.{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1986|p=12}} Haas earned a M.S. (1949) and Ph.D. (1951) in mathematics from the [[MIT Department of Mathematics]] (MIT).{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1986|p=12}} Her dissertation was titled ''Singular perturbations of an ordinary differential equation''. [[Norman Levinson]] was her doctoral advisor.{{sfn|Haas|1951|p=}} She met her future husband, {{Interlanguage link|Felix Haas (mathematician)|lt=Felix Haas|qid=Q95299428}}, a fellow mathematician at MIT.{{sfn|Purdue University Archives and Special Collections}} Haas was selected as an [[American Association of University Women]] Vassie James Hill Fellow in 1951.{{sfn|''The Indianapolis Star''|1986|p=55}}{{sfn|Purdue University Archives and Special Collections}} She was a member of [[Phi Beta Kappa]], [[Sigma Xi]], and [[Eta Kappa Nu]].{{sfn|''The Indianapolis Star''|1986|p=55}}

== Career ==
Haas was a lecturer at [[Immaculata College]] from 1952 to 1955 and an instructor at the [[University of Connecticut]] from 1955 to 1956.{{sfn|''The Indianapolis Star''|1986|p=55}} She was a faculty member at the [[University of Detroit]] from 1957 to 1962.{{sfn|''The Indianapolis Star''|1986|p=55}} Haas also taught at [[Wayne State University]].{{sfn|Purdue University Archives and Special Collections}}

She joined the faculty at [[Purdue University]] in January 1962{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1986|p=12}} as an assistant professor in the college of electrical engineering and computer engineering.{{sfn|Purdue University Archives and Special Collections}} By 1978, Haas was a full professor of electrical engineering in the [[Purdue University College of Engineering]].{{sfn|Purdue University Archives and Special Collections}}{{sfn|''The Indianapolis Star''|1986|p=55}} Her areas of expertise included [[optimal control]], [[nonlinear control]], and [[optimal estimation]].{{sfn|''The Indianapolis Star''|1986|p=55}} Due to nepotism rules (her husband was a fellow mathematician), Haas took a position in electrical engineering rather than mathematics.{{sfn|Coxson|1986|p=2}}

Haas advocated for [[women in STEM fields]]. Some of her earlier academic environments were hostile to women.{{sfn|Coxson|1986|p=2}} In a few instances, she was the only department member excluded from grant proposals. This had largely improved by the early 1980s.{{sfn|Coxson|1986|p=2}} For 15 years, Haas was the counselor of the Purdue University student chapter of the [[Society of Women Engineers]].{{sfn|Coxson|1986|p=2}}

Haas joined the [[Association for Women in Mathematics]] in 1975, serving as a coordinator for the speakers' bureau.{{sfn|Coxson|1986|p=2}} She was a member of the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE) committee on professional opportunities for women and the [[American Society for Engineering Education]] (ASEE) constituent committee on women in engineering.{{sfn|Coxson|1986|p=2}} For Haas' support and encouragement of women students in engineering, in 1977, she was elected as one of five "Very Important Women" on campus by the Association of Women Students.{{sfn|Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|1986|p=10}} In 1977, Haas received the D.D. Ewing Award as an outstanding teacher in the  Purdue School of Electrical Engineering.{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1978|p=6}} She received the 1978 Helen B. Schleman Medallion Award for her service and encouragement of women in academic and professional areas.{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1978|p=6}} In the 1970s, Haas was a nominee for the distinguished science award of the Society of Women Engineers.{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1978|p=6}}

From 1983 to 1984, Haas was a visiting professor at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] through the [[National Science Foundation]] visiting professorships for women program. In this position, she was a full time researcher investigating [[control theory]] and infinite dimensional control problems.{{sfn|Coxson|1986|p=2}}

Haas was active in the [[Control engineering|control systems]] community and was on the program committee of the [[American Control Conference]]. She was also the [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics]] (SIAM) representative to the  IEEE conference on decision and control.{{sfn|Coxson|1986|p=2}} Mathematician and colleague [[Pamela G. Coxson]] stated that Haas' involvement "increased the participation of the mathematical community in these two annual conferences."{{sfn|Coxson|1986|p=2}} She is included in biographical listings of ''[[Who's Who in the Midwest]]'', ''Who's Who of American Women'', and ''[[American Men and Women of Science]]''.{{sfn|Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|1986|p=10}} She was a former editor of the ''Women in Engineering Students Newsletter''.{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1986|p=12}} Haas was a member of the American Association of University Women,{{sfn|Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|1986|p=10}}  [[League of Women Voters]], [[YWCA]], and served on the board of directors of the Lafayette Symphony.{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1986|p=12}}{{sfn|''The Indianapolis Star''|1986|p=55}}

Haas and sociologist [[Carolyn C. Perrucci]] co-edited the book {{Cite book |title=[[Women in Scientific and Engineering Professions]] |date=1984 |publisher=[[University of Michigan Press]] |isbn=978-0-472-10049-1 |language=en}}{{sfn|Purdue University Archives and Special Collections}}

Eight months after leaving MIT in 1984, Haas was diagnosed with a brain tumor and was soon unconscious.{{sfn|Coxson|1986|p=2}}

== Personal life ==
Haas resided in [[West Lafayette, Indiana]].{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1986|p=12}} She was married to Felix Haas.{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1986|p=12}} They had a daughter and two sons.{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1986|p=12}}

Haas was unconscious from a [[brain tumor]] from 1984 until her death on the morning of January 21, 1986, at St. Elizabeth Hospital.{{sfn|''Journal & Courier''|1986|p=12}}{{sfn|Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|1986|p=10}}

In 1990, the Council on the Status of Women at Purdue University established Violet B. Haas award that recognizes people who promote the status of women at the university.{{sfn|Purdue University Archives and Special Collections}}
